soil-water-124.title: Wetlands, where the soil runs out of air
soil-water-124.text: Wetlands grow on every continent except Antarctica, from the Amazon basin and the West Siberian Plain to the Pantanal and the Sundarbans. A wetland is a semi-aquatic ecosystem whose ground is flooded or saturated, permanently or seasonally. Its soils therefore run short of oxygen, the condition traced in {{ref:soil-water-218}}. Wetlands sit between open water and dry land, and their plants' roots are adapted to that oxygen-poor, waterlogged ground. One short definition calls a wetland a community of water-loving plants rooted in the saturated soil described in {{ref:soil-water-119}}. There are four main kinds. {{ref:soil-water-129}} carries herbaceous plants, and {{ref:soil-water-134}} carries woody ones. {{ref:soil-water-121}} and {{ref:soil-water-125}} are both peat-forming. About 60% of the world's wetlands are made of peat. Wetlands can also be sorted by where their water comes from: tides, the mixed tide and river water of estuaries, rivers overflowing their banks, or rain and meltwater. The US Cowardin system names five types: marine, estuarine, riverine, lacustrine and the inland kind in {{ref:soil-water-152}}. US regulations define wetlands as land wet often and long enough to support plants adapted to saturated soil. That kind of soil is part of the legal test. In 2005 the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment found wetlands more threatened than any other ecosystem. Since 1971 {{ref:soil-water-262}} has protected those of international importance.

soil-water-136.title: Peatlands, wetlands built from their own dead plants
soil-water-136.text: Peat more than 10 m deep is common in temperate regions, and in the tropics it can pass 25 m. A peatland is a wetland whose soil consists of organic matter from decaying plants, laid down in layers of {{ref:soil-class-070}}. It arises where waterlogging cuts off oxygen, so plant litter only partly decomposes. Ecologists apply the term to any ground with peat at least 30 cm deep, even ground that has been completely drained. Precipitation and temperature mainly control where peat forms. Relief matters too, because flat ground and basins waterlog easily. Where organic matter stays waterlogged, topography, climate, parent material, living things and time together shape the result. Peat usually starts in one of three ways: forest on mineral soil slowly waterlogs, a lake fills in, or peat forms directly on bare ground left by glaciers. As it accumulates, peat lifts the ground above the original topography. Peat also has a high cation-exchange capacity. It swaps cations such as Ca²⁺ for H⁺, so water passing through loses nutrients and its pH falls. Peatlands are therefore acidic unless plenty of groundwater flows in. They cover about 3% of the globe's surface. Around a quarter of that area serves agriculture and forestry, which means ditches to lower the water table.

soil-water-115.title: Landscape ecology, reading land as a patchwork
soil-water-115.text: In 1939 the German geographer Carl Troll used aerial photographs to study how environment and vegetation interact, and coined a word for the work: Landschaftsökologie. Landscape ecology is the science of how ecological processes relate to particular ecosystems across a range of landscape scales and spatial patterns. It treats a landscape as an uneven area of interacting patches, from forests, grasslands and lakes to farmland and towns. Traditional ecology often assumes a uniform system. Landscape ecology instead builds on differences across space and time, and its hallmark is the link between pattern, process and scale. By 1980 it was an established discipline, and the International Association for Landscape Ecology was founded in 1982. Its tools are remote sensing, GIS and models. One application estimates how much carbon a region's soils hold from landform, vegetation types and rainfall data. It also draws on geomorphology, the study of how geological formations give a landscape its structure. Humans count explicitly as agents that change landscapes, and the field proposes ways to restore degraded ones.

soil-water-119.title: Hydric soil, the ground that drowns
soil-water-119.text: When rain or flooding fills every pore, gas moves through soil some 10,000 times more slowly. Most soils are aerobic. Roots, most microorganisms and animals such as earthworms need oxygen, which travels through the connected pores described in {{ref:soil-phys-069}}. Saturation closes those passages. If anaerobic conditions last long in the growing season, different biological and chemical reactions take over from those of aerobic soils. Saturation that is prolonged and repeated over many years leaves distinctive properties that can be recognized in the field. Soils with them are called hydric soils: soils permanently or seasonally saturated until they turn anaerobic, as in wetlands. They may occupy only a small part of a landscape, yet they keep important soil functions. Their plants often have aerenchyma, internal air spaces that carry oxygen down to the roots. Rich hydric soils line the waterbodies where the wetlands of {{ref:soil-water-134}} and {{ref:soil-water-129}} form. A Gleysol is one kind: a hydric soil saturated by groundwater long enough to develop a characteristic gleyic color pattern.

soil-water-129.title: Marshes, the grassy wetlands at the water's edge
soil-water-129.text: Marsh plants root in wet mud with little oxygen, so many grow aerenchyma, air channels that carry air down to their roots. A marsh is a wetland dominated by herbaceous rather than woody plants. More loosely, the word means any low-lying, seasonally waterlogged ground. In Europe and in farming literature it also covers meadows needing drainage and embanked land. Marshes often edge lakes and streams, a transition between aquatic and land ecosystems. Vegetation sets them apart: {{ref:soil-water-134}} is dominated by trees, while peat-forming wetlands have built up deposits of acidic peat. Marsh pH tends to be neutral to alkaline, unlike the acid conditions under which peat accumulates in rain-fed wetlands. The three main types differ mainly in location and salinity: {{ref:soil-fert-144}}, freshwater tidal marshes, and the inland kind in {{ref:soil-water-146}}. The salty type flourishes on sheltered, tide-washed coasts where sediment builds up faster than the land sinks. Marshes hold 0.1% of global sequestered land carbon. Most natural marshland is threatened by sea level rise and the erosion it brings.

soil-water-134.title: Swamps, where trees stand in water
soil-water-134.text: The largest swamp on Earth spreads across the ground the Amazon River floods. Other giants line the Mississippi and the Congo. A swamp is a forested wetland, with saturated soils or standing water dominated by woody plants that tolerate water. It is a transition zone shaped by both land and water, and its water may be fresh, brackish or seawater. Freshwater swamps form along large rivers or lakes, and rain and seasonal floods drive their natural swings in water level. Saltwater swamps line tropical and subtropical coasts. Slow-moving water feeds them from precipitation, groundwater, tides and freshwater floods. That hydrology controls their chemistry, including oxygen, nutrients, pH and toxicity. As water moves through, the swamp filters out nutrients, sediment and pollutants, and excess chemicals end up buried in the bottom sediment. The two main types are true swamps, or swamp forests, and the transitional kind in {{ref:soil-water-148}}. Some swamps are peatlands, such as {{ref:soil-water-267}}. Swamps have higher pH and more available nutrients than the rain-fed peat wetlands of {{ref:soil-water-121}}.

soil-fert-144.title: Salt marshes, built by plants that trap mud
soil-fert-144.text: A salt marsh begins as a bare tidal flat. Sediment settles until plants can colonize it, and the plants then trap and bind still more. The result is a tidal wetland in the upper intertidal zone, regularly flooded by seawater or brackish water and dominated by salt-tolerant halophytes. Heavy sedimentation and abundant organic matter keep its sediments reliably anoxic, an ideal home for sulfate-reducing bacteria. Bacteria and fungi drive nutrient cycling by remineralizing organic matter, and bacteria degrade up to 88% of the lignocellulose. Nitrifiers such as Nitrosomonas and Nitrosospira, and nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria, are common in the mud.

soil-water-264.title: Floodplains, where rivers lay down new land
soil-water-264.text: A floodplain holds far more sediment than the river that feeds it carries. It is the land beside a river, from the channel banks to the valley sides, that floods when discharge is high. Its soils are flood-laid clays, silts, sands and gravels, the {{ref:soil-form-112}} that regular floods refresh with nutrients. The Nile and Mississippi basins farm their floodplains heavily. Most floodplains grow sideways: point bars build on the insides of meanders while the outer bank erodes, a process called lateral accretion. They also grow upward. On undisturbed rivers, water spills over the banks every one to two years and leaves a thin veneer of sediment, coarsest and thickest by the channel. This is vertical accretion. Most sand drops on natural levees beside the channel, while silt and clay settle farther out as floodplain mud. Every 10–1000 years a river may abandon its channel belt and build a new one elsewhere, a process called avulsion. An abandoned floodplain may survive as a raised step beside the valley. Draining floodplains or narrowing them with levees weakens their flood control, so floods become more severe.

soil-water-145.title: Ombrotrophic, living on rain alone
soil-water-145.text: The word means 'cloud-fed', from the Greek ómbros, rain, and trophē, food. Ombrotrophic soils or vegetation get all their water and nutrients from precipitation, not from streams or springs. Such sites are cut off hydrologically from the surrounding landscape. Rain is acidic and very low in nutrients, so they host organisms that tolerate acid, nutrient-poor conditions. Climate runs the system: precipitation supplies water and nutrients, and temperature sets how fast water evaporates. The effect can override even nutrient-rich rock. In high-rainfall areas, limestone boulders may be capped by acidic peat vegetation. The rain-fed wetlands of {{ref:soil-water-121}} rely solely on precipitation and atmospheric dust, though their slowly decaying peat releases some zinc, copper and manganese. Mercury and lead stay put in their peat, so they keep a record of past mercury deposition. High nitrogen deposition in Europe has shifted their plants toward more vascular growth and less Sphagnum, the moss that holds moisture and nutrients and aids carbon storage.

soil-water-121.title: Bogs, the acid wetlands that keep their dead
soil-water-121.text: Bodies buried in bogs thousands of years ago have come out preserved, because low oxygen, high acidity and tannic acids hold back decay. A bog is a wetland that accumulates peat, a deposit of dead plant material, often sphagnum moss. It is one of the four main wetland types, and its peat is typically over 30 centimetres thick. Bogs take most of their water and nutrients from precipitation, as {{ref:soil-water-145}} explains, so they are nutrient-poor and strongly acidic. Unlike {{ref:soil-water-125}}, they get little mineral-rich ground or surface water. Rain lacks the calcium, magnesium and carbonate that would buffer the acidity of carbon dioxide from the air. Plants grow slowly, but decay is slower still in the oxygen-poor, saturated soil. So peat piles up, sometimes many metres deep. Most bogs form in cooler northern climates in poorly draining lake basins. Quaking bogs are floating sphagnum mats about half a metre thick, anchored by sedges, that move underfoot. Undisturbed bogs take up and store carbon. Once the peat is extracted, the wetland is hard to restore, because peat accumulates slowly.

soil-water-139.title: Muskeg, the northern peat that swallows machines
soil-water-139.text: Heavy equipment has sunk into muskeg when the frozen ground thawed in spring. Muskeg is a peat-forming ecosystem of northern, mostly Arctic and boreal climates, roughly the same thing as a bog or peatland. The term is standard in Canada and Alaska and comes from the Cree maskēk, 'low-lying marsh'. It forms where permafrost, clay or bedrock blocks drainage so that rain and snowmelt collect, and it needs abundant rain and cool summers. Low oxygen and cool temperatures hold back bacteria and fungi, so plant debris decays slowly and builds up as peat. Sphagnum holds fifteen to thirty times its own weight in water, so muskeg can form even on slopes, and it can exceed 30 metres deep. Wet, acidic and relatively infertile, with the water table near the surface, it cannot grow large trees. Uncleared muskeg buckles when it freezes, so people cross it on log corduroy roads or cheaper winter ice roads.

soil-water-144.title: Polders, land held dry behind dikes
soil-water-144.text: The Dutch have turned wet ground into some 3,000 polders, and as much as 20% of the Netherlands has at some time been reclaimed from the sea. A polder is a low-lying tract enclosed by dikes, an artificial hydrological unit. It may be reclaimed lake bed or seabed, a floodplain cut off by a dike, or a marsh diked and then drained. Water keeps arriving through seepage, rainfall, rivers and canals, so it must be pumped out or let out through sluices at low tide. Drained ground subsides, and peat polders sink as their peat decomposes in air. Eventually every polder lies below the surrounding water some or all of the time.

soil-water-143.title: Slumps, when a hillside slides and tips back
soil-water-143.text: After heavy rain a hillside can let go as a single block. A slump is a form of {{ref:soil-water-053}} in which a coherent mass of loosely consolidated material or rock moves a short distance down a slope. Rain both lubricates the material and adds to its weight, which is why slumps often follow storms. In a rotational slump the block slides on a concave-upward surface and rotates backward, so its original surface becomes less steep. Translational slumps move on planes such as joints or bedding, especially where a permeable layer lies over an impermeable one. A cliff-like scarp marks where the mass broke away. Back-tilted block tops can hold ponds or swampy ground, and uneven ridges form near the toe. Earthquakes, thorough wetting, freezing and thawing, undercutting and loading can all set one off. A common trigger is removing the slope's base by stream or wave erosion or by road building. Speeds range from metres per second to metres per year. Sudden slumps may stabilize within hours, but most take months or years. Added water and lost cohesion at the toe can turn slumping material into an earthflow. On steep hillsides slumps often follow fracture zones in clay, and much stream-bank erosion happens as weakened banks fail in large slumps.

soil-water-147.title: Minerotrophic, fed by water that has touched rock
soil-water-147.text: Water that has seeped through rock arrives carrying a load. Minerotrophic environments get their nutrients mainly from such groundwater, flowing through mineral-rich soil or rock, or from surface water flowing over land. Its dissolved chemicals raise nutrient levels and reduce acidity. Where they include bases such as calcium or magnesium ions, the water is called base-rich, in the sense of {{ref:soil-chem-054}}, and is neutral or alkaline. The peat wetland of {{ref:soil-water-125}} is often minerotrophic, especially in its richer forms, while bogs and its poorest forms are often ombrotrophic. Marshes and swamps may also be partly fed by groundwater. The ions a wetland's water brings set its pH, conductivity and nutrient levels. These differ between sites where groundwater discharges and sites where it recharges, and they change with seasonal groundwater levels. Geology, soil type and surface form shape a wetland too. A steady groundwater supply supports diverse plants. It also lets peat accumulate, provided the water does not flow too fast. The terms minerogenous and geogenous often serve as synonyms, though they refer mainly to hydrology, and minerotrophic to nutrients.

soil-water-125.title: Fens, the peat wetlands fed from below
soil-water-125.text: Fens tend to lie over calcium-rich rocks such as limestone, and the rock shows in their water. A fen is a peat-accumulating wetland fed by mineral-rich ground or surface water. It is one of the main wetland types alongside marshes, swamps and bogs, and fens and bogs, both peat-forming, are grouped together as {{ref:soil-water-137}}. That water input gives fens higher mineral concentrations and a more basic pH than bogs. The chemistry of the groundwater, set by the rocks it passes through, controls the pH. The water table sits at or near the surface, so fen soils stay inundated, and oxygen diffuses in so slowly that they are anaerobic. An estimated 1.1 million square kilometres of fen exist worldwide. As peat builds up it can cut off the groundwater, so a fen turns rain-fed and more acidic and may become a bog. Draining a fen dries and aerates the peat, which then decomposes or even burns. Whether fens are net sinks or net sources of greenhouse gases is still disputed, because microbes in their oxygen-free soils produce methane.

soil-water-263.title: Riparian zones, the living edge of a stream
soil-water-263.text: Thin the plants along a stream and its water grows warmer and swings more in temperature. The riparian zone is the strip of land where a river or stream meets the land around it. Its water-loving plants matter for conserving soil, for biodiversity and the health of aquatic ecosystems. The zone acts as a natural biofilter, shielding the water from excess sediment, polluted surface runoff and erosion. Meanders, plants and roots slow the water, reducing soil erosion and flood damage, and trapped sediment replenishes soils and builds banks. The zone also lowers nitrate from manure and fertilizer in runoff, largely by denitrification, and wet riparian zones remove it especially fast. Where streamside ground holds standing water or saturated soil for a season, it is normally called a wetland because of its hydric soils. Zones damaged by building, farming or forestry are usually restored through erosion control and replanting.

soil-water-146.title: Freshwater marshes and their dark, slow-rotting soils
soil-water-146.text: Black or brown, wet and rich in organic matter: that is the soil of a freshwater marsh. Such a marsh is non-forested, with shallow fresh water that floods it continuously or often. It usually lies near a river mouth, along a lake, or in poorly drained low ground such as an abandoned oxbow lake. Most of its water comes from the surface. Its soils are hydric, saturated in the growing season. Decomposition is slow, so organic matter builds up. Microbes use up the oxygen, and anaerobic processes then accumulate or deplete reduced iron and other minerals, giving the soils a distinctive morphology. Types include river, lake, tidal freshwater and depressional marshes, the last often fed by springs or seepage.

soil-water-126.title: From bog to rich fen, a gradient set by calcium
soil-water-126.text: In wetland science, 'rich' and 'poor' count species, not money. Species richness depends strongly on pH and on calcium and bicarbonate concentrations. Bogs and fens line up along a gradient: bogs at the poor end, extremely rich fens at the rich end, and poor fens between. Rich fens are strongly minerotrophic, fed by water dominated by calcium and bicarbonate, and run neutral to slightly acidic, about pH 7 to 5. Groundwater passing limestone dissolves some calcium carbonate. The bicarbonate it produces buffers the fen and keeps its pH relatively stable. In extreme rich fens, often pH 7 or above, calcium carbonate settles out as marl when plants or the atmosphere draw down dissolved carbon dioxide. Rich does not always mean productive, though: at high concentrations calcium binds phosphate. Poor fens, about pH 5.5 to 4, have thicker peat that cuts plants off from the mineral soil below and weakens groundwater buffering. They also form where groundwater flows through weakly buffering sediments such as sand. Sphagnum mosses acidify fens, and their spread can turn a rich fen into a poor one.

soil-water-127.title: How wetland soils pass nutrients between two worlds
soil-water-127.text: Most wetland soils come in two layers. A thin oxygenated layer sits over a reduced one, and microbes adapted to each oxidize and reduce nutrients as they cycle between them. Wetland nutrient cycling is the movement of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and other elements through soils at this boundary, driven by the chemistry of {{ref:soil-chem-113}}. The reduced layer hosts denitrification, the reduction of manganese, iron and sulfate, and methanogenesis. Organic carbon has three fates: it is respired to CO2, buried as peat or decomposed to methane. Peat builds up where plant production exceeds decomposition. Methanogenic archaea in anaerobic peat make methane from CO2 and hydrogen, and sedge and brown-moss fens emit more of it than sphagnum bogs. Nitrogen shuttles between the layers. Ammonium from anaerobic decay diffuses up and is nitrified in the oxidized layer. The nitrate diffuses back down and is denitrified to nitrogen gas and some nitrous oxide. Nitrogen and phosphorus limit wetland fertility, and almost all phosphorus arrives in sediment or plant litter from other ecosystems. Iron can bind phosphate to toxic levels, but peat supplies organic anions that iron binds instead. Because wetlands are hotspots and sinks for these transformations, they can be built on purpose to treat nutrient-rich water.

soil-water-122.title: Raised bogs, domes of peat that outgrow the groundwater
soil-water-122.text: European raised bogs have been growing for about 11,000 years, roughly a millimetre a year. A raised bog is an acidic, mineral-poor bog fed only by precipitation, its peat risen into a dome above the groundwater. Many begin as fens. Lack of oxygen and high acidity stop decay, peat builds up, and the bog rises above the groundwater until rain alone feeds it. Rootless peat mosses grow upward while their lower layers turn to peat. A living upper acrotelm, where new organic matter forms, lies over the saturated, less active catotelm, and light white peat lies over well-humified black peat. Growth needs precipitation that exceeds losses to discharge and evaporation and falls evenly through the year. The dome is typically a few metres high, often fringed by fen where groundwater seeps in at the edges or along streams. Peat cutting and mineral pollution from farms and industry badly threaten raised bogs. Their last great regions are in western Siberia and Canada.

soil-water-149.title: Paludification, how dry forest turns to peatland
soil-water-149.text: Most boreal peatlands did not begin in a lake. They crept over dry land. Paludification is the build-up of peat on previously drier, vegetated mineral soil, turning forest, grassland or bare land into peatland. Organic soil starts and thickens over inorganic soil with no fully aquatic phase. Peat can also start as a lake fills in, but paludification is the most common route in the boreal zone. It requires a wet water balance in the growing season, with precipitation exceeding evapotranspiration plus runoff. Climate, geomorphology, geology and soils usually control that balance, though local peat accumulation alone can also drive the process. Tree removal, forest fires, natural or human-caused, more precipitation and podzolization can all tip the balance. Flat, low-slope ground helps, as in the world's two largest peatlands, the West Siberian Plain and the Hudson/James Bay Lowlands. Heavy clay acts as an impermeable floor that lets water collect, and surface water from melting permafrost can speed things up. Once under way in boreal forest, paludification lowers soil temperature, aeration, nutrient availability and decomposition rates. It can even lead to new permafrost.

soil-water-138.title: Peatlands, the largest carbon store on land
soil-water-138.text: Peatlands cover just 3% of Earth's land, yet they hold between 500 and 700 billion tonnes of carbon. That is over half the amount in the atmosphere, and it makes them the largest natural carbon store on land. Plants take in CO2 at the surface, while living plants and decaying peat respire some back out. The water table is the main control. A high one submerges peat and slows respiration. A falling one, as in drought, speeds aerobic decomposition and CO2 release. Water level also sets the size of two zones: methane-making microbes in the anoxic peat below, and methane-oxidizing ones above. In one Alaskan study, methane flux varied by as much as 300% between seasons. Natural peat-forming wetlands are a small CO2 sink but generally net emitters of methane and nitrous oxide. Over millennia they have still had a net cooling effect. Draining one lets oxygen into the peat, and a store that was taking up carbon becomes a net emitter. Northern peatlands built up mostly in the Holocene, after the Pleistocene glaciers retreated. Estimates of their carbon vary widely, from 415 Gt to 1055 Gt.

soil-water-132.title: Prairie potholes, the ponds the glaciers left
soil-water-132.text: Glaciers once covered the plains of northern North America, and they left shallow depressions behind in great numbers. Each spring those hollows fill with water. A prairie pothole is a marsh in one of them. Some hold water only for a season, while others stay wet all year. Small as they are, such wetlands can contribute significantly to recharging regional groundwater. They are also important breeding habitat for many species of waterfowl.

soil-water-131.title: Vernal pools, ponds that vanish by summer
soil-water-131.text: No fish live in a vernal pool, which is why many amphibians breed there in spring. A vernal pool is a seasonal marsh in a shallow depression that holds water in winter and spring and may be completely dry by summer and fall. It forms where an impermeable or very slowly permeable layer, such as a duripan, claypan or lava flow, underlies a small hollow and perches the water table. It drains only internally, cut off from perennial inflow, yet holds ponded water at least briefly in most years. In California such pools often fill the hollows between {{ref:soil-water-133}}, on old, strongly developed soils.

soil-water-130.title: Wet meadows, flooded often yet dry in summer
soil-water-130.text: Wet meadows often hold very high plant diversity and dense stores of buried seeds. A wet meadow is a freshwater marsh that floods regularly but is often dry in summer. It occupies shallow lake basins, low-lying depressions, the ground between shallow marshes and uplands, and the edges of large lakes and rivers. As it matures, decomposing vegetation thickens the soil into raised mounds above the water. Shrubs and small trees take root there, a route toward {{ref:soil-water-148}}.

openers.soils-in-the-landscape: Soil changes character where water lingers. Ground flooded or saturated, permanently or for a season, runs short of oxygen, and its soils turn anaerobic. Some of these wetlands are grassy, some forested, and some are washed by the tides. Others pile dead plants into layers of peat, fed by rain alone or by streams and springs, and in the cold north those peat-forming lands stretch across Arctic and boreal climates. This chapter follows soil through such places, from river land that floods at high water to ground enclosed by dikes, and uses a science of landscape patterns to see how they fit together.
